question: What is the 'ladder' for improving a model's results?
answers: Fine-tune first, then prompt, then RAG
Prompt first, then RAG, then fine-tune
RAG first, then fine-tune, then prompt
Fine-tune, then RAG, then prompting
fact: Climb only as high as the problem needs. Prompting is cheapest and quickest to change, RAG adds knowledge, and fine-tuning is the heaviest step.

question: Which job is fine-tuning best suited to?
answers: Teaching it this week's price list
Letting staff see only their files
Adding citations to every claim
A consistent house style or format
fact: Fine-tuning shifts the weights towards a habit: a tone, a format, or a specialist classification. It is not the tool for facts that keep changing.

question: A customer wants to fine-tune on all their documents. What do they usually need?
answers: RAG, to answer from their documents
A bigger context window alone
More GPUs for faster training
A fine-tune on a larger document set
fact: RAG gives the model knowledge, fine-tuning gives it habits. It is an open-book exam versus years of practice. Usually the goal is answering from documents, so start with RAG and a small eval set.

question: A customer asks, 'What is an eval?' Best answer?
answers: A cost report for monthly usage
A summary of customer feedback
A test set that scores model answers
A safety certificate from the vendor
fact: Collect real inputs with a view of what good looks like, then score the model against them. It lets you compare models fairly and catch problems when something changes.

question: A customer wants a cheaper model for one narrow task. What does distillation do?
answers: Compresses documents into smaller chunks
Removes private data from training sets
Trains a small model to copy a big one
Merges two models into one bigger model
fact: A big model's outputs teach a smaller, cheaper one a narrow task. Handy when you want near-big-model quality at small-model cost and speed.

question: A customer asks what a golden set is. Best answer?
answers: Real questions with known good answers
The best-performing prompts found so far
A list of approved customers
The model's highest-rated replies
fact: A set of perhaps 50 to 500 real questions with known answers and sources, including tricky ones and questions that should be refused. It is the yardstick for everything else.

question: What does 'human in the loop' mean?
answers: A person writes every prompt by hand
A person retrains the model nightly
A person replaces the model in a crisis
A person reviews risky output first
fact: For high-stakes outputs, like financial advice or contract changes, someone checks before anything goes out. The model drafts; the person decides.

question: A customer asks what a guardrail is. Best answer?
answers: A rule that makes every answer longer
A check around the model to cut harm
A faster path for all trusted users
A cheaper way to store old prompts
fact: Guardrails are checkpoints on the way in, during retrieval, on the way out and before actions. No single one is enough, so use layers.

question: What is a system prompt?
answers: The user's first question in a chat
Standing instructions for its role
A prompt saved for the next user
A log of every earlier prompt
fact: It is the standing brief given before the conversation: the model's role, tone and rules. It is the cheapest lever for steering behaviour.

question: What does a groundedness check test?
answers: The answer is short enough
The reply matches the brand tone
The answer arrives within a few seconds
Every claim is backed by the sources
fact: It asks whether each statement in the answer can be found in the retrieved passages. Unsupported claims are the telltale sign of a guess.

question: A customer quotes a leaderboard. What do you steer to?
answers: A test on their own real data
A bigger leaderboard comparison
A vendor's marketing slide deck
A poll of what peers are using
fact: Benchmarks move monthly and rarely match a specific business task. A golden set from the customer's own tickets shows how a model does on their work.

question: Which evaluation question does recall@k answer?
answers: Did the answer sound polite?
Was the reply under the token cap?
Was the right chunk in the top k?
Did the user click thumbs up?
fact: It scores the retrieval step alone: out of the top five chunks, was the one holding the answer there? If not, even the best model cannot save the reply.

question: What should you do before trusting an LLM judge?
answers: Let it grade its own earlier answers
Give it the cheapest model available
Compare its grades with human ones
Turn its temperature up for fairness
fact: A judge model with a clear rubric scales well, but test it against people first. Cheap code checks come first, then a judge, then human review on a sample.

question: When should offline evals be rerun?
answers: After any change to prompt or model
Once, before the first launch
When a customer happens to complain
Once a year, at the contract renewal
fact: Treat it like a test suite: rerun on every change to the prompt, model, chunking or embeddings, and block the release if scores drop.

question: What makes a pilot more than a science project?
answers: A very large number of test users
The newest model on every task
A launch event for the whole firm
Success criteria agreed up front
fact: Define what good looks like before anyone writes a prompt: an owner, a measure, a baseline, a time box, and what happens if it succeeds.

question: Narrow fine-tuning can do what to the model?
answers: Wipe its general knowledge
Make it worse at other tasks
Raise its context window limit
Make its answers much longer
fact: Training hard on a narrow set can erode other skills, and bad examples teach bad habits quickly. Compare against the base model with a good prompt before deploying.

question: What matters most in fine-tuning data?
answers: Sheer volume of any text
Good, consistent example pairs
Facts that change every week
Whole documents, unlabelled
fact: Examples are inputs paired with ideal outputs. A smaller set of consistent, good ones usually beats a big messy one. Hold some back to test the result.

question: Which guardrail belongs at the output stage?
answers: A redaction step on the user's prompt
A permission filter on search results
Approval before the refund is issued
A grounding check on the answer
fact: Before an answer goes out you can run moderation, a personal-data leak check, a grounding check and format validation. Each layer catches what the others miss.

question: A customer says 'make it more accurate'. First step?
answers: Agree what 'good' means and test it
Switch to the largest model available
Fine-tune on all their documents
Add more guardrails everywhere
fact: You cannot improve what you have not measured. A small eval set built from real tickets turns 'make it better' into a number you can track.

question: How does a team reduce human review over time?
answers: Remove it once the launch is complete
Keep it constant for every output
Ease off as evals show reliability
Replace it with a longer prompt
fact: Start with more review, then reduce it where measured results prove the system reliable. Keep it for the cases where an error is costly.

question: A better base model is released. What about your fine-tune?
answers: Keep it, as tuned models never go stale
Fine-tune again on the same data
Re-test, as the tune may not be needed
Delete the eval set to save time
fact: A stronger base model can erase the gain from a fine-tune. Rebaseline against the new model plus a good prompt, and keep the tune only if it still wins.

question: Staff pick the better of two replies each time. Which tuning fits?
answers: Preference fine-tuning
Retrieval over past replies
Distilling a smaller model
A longer system prompt
fact: Preference tuning learns from better-versus-worse pairs, which suits 'like this, not that' tone choices. Still try prompting first and compare against it.

question: Why keep questions that should be refused in a golden set?
answers: They make the set look bigger
They test how fast the model replies
They lower the cost of each run
Good systems know when to decline
fact: A set holding only answerable questions cannot catch a bot that confidently answers things it should refuse. Include tricky and out-of-scope questions too.

question: What do online evals add to offline tests?
answers: A way to skip the golden set entirely
Real-use signals, such as thumbs
A cheaper way to train the model
Automatic fixes of wrong answers
fact: Offline tests protect each release; online signals show what real users do afterwards: thumbs up or down, sampled reviews, A/B tests and drift monitoring.

question: Which task suits reinforcement fine-tuning?
answers: Open questions with no right answer
Tasks with a score you can check
Tasks that need up-to-date facts
Writing in a friendlier tone
fact: It needs a grader that scores each output, so it fits tasks you can check automatically, such as code that passes tests, maths or classification.

question: What is an A/B test for two prompts?
answers: Ask the model which one it prefers
Score both for spelling and tone
Compare two versions in real use
Run both on a single test question
fact: Split real traffic between version A and B and compare a chosen measure, such as resolution rate. It shows what works in real use, not just in the lab.

question: What is 'drift' in a live AI system?
answers: The model moving to a new data centre
Answers getting steadily shorter
Quality slipping as inputs change
Prompts drifting into other languages
fact: Customers, products and policies change, so yesterday's test set can stop matching today's questions. Monitor and refresh the evals.

question: What does a moderation layer do?
answers: Picks the cheapest model per task
Compresses long prompts to save cost
Screens inputs and outputs
Rewrites replies to be shorter
fact: A moderation layer is a separate check on what goes in and what comes out. It is one of several guardrails, not the only one.

question: Why add a moderation layer if the model has safety training?
answers: Safety training fades after launch
It makes answers more creative
No single check catches everything
It replaces the system prompt
fact: No single check is perfect. Input checks, safe retrieval, output checks and human approval each catch different problems.

question: How do you keep a golden set useful over time?
answers: Delete questions the model passes
Add new real failures as they appear
Replace it with synthetic questions
Shuffle the answer keys monthly
fact: Each real failure is a free test case. Adding them keeps the set matched to how people actually use the system.

question: Prompt A scores 8 of 10 and B scores 7 of 10. What's fair to say?
answers: A wins, so adopt it now
B wins if it is run again
Ten cases are too few to tell
Both are guaranteed identical
fact: Small test sets are noisy. Use enough real cases, and look at where the two differ, before declaring a winner.

question: What is 'shadow mode' for a new AI assistant?
answers: It hides answers from every user
It runs outside office hours
It drafts answers nobody acts on
It copies a rival's best prompts
fact: The assistant produces answers in the background and people compare them with what they actually did. You gain evidence before anyone depends on it.

question: A bot fails 20% of test cases. What is the best next step?
answers: Switch to the biggest model
Add more rules to the prompt
Group failures into patterns
Retrain on the whole test set
fact: Reading the failures usually shows two or three causes, such as missing documents or unclear instructions. Fix the biggest cause first and retest.

question: An LLM judge keeps preferring longer answers. What is this?
answers: A sign the longer answers are better
A bias to check against people
A fault in the search index
A temperature setting error
fact: Judges can favour length or style. Compare their grades with human ones on a sample, and adjust the rubric before relying on them.

question: Why keep prompts under version control?
answers: So they cost less to run each time
So the model remembers them for good
So any user can edit them live
So changes can be tested or undone
fact: A prompt is part of the product. Versioning shows what changed when results moved and lets you roll back safely.

question: Offline scores are high but live thumbs-down is rising. Likely cause?
answers: The thumbs buttons are misreporting
The model became more creative
Embeddings have run out of space
Real questions have moved on
fact: A fixed test set only covers what you thought of. Online signals show new kinds of question, which you then add to the offline set.

question: Which eval check is cheapest and most reliable where it applies?
answers: An LLM judge on every answer
A code check, such as a format test
A panel of senior staff
A public leaderboard score
fact: If a rule can be tested by code, such as valid format or a required field, do that first. Save judges and humans for what code cannot check.

question: Replies are accurate but too casual for a bank. Next rung?
answers: Fine-tune straight away
Tighten the prompt with examples
Add a vector database
Switch to a bigger reasoning model
fact: Tone is a behaviour problem, and the ladder starts with prompting. Examples of the desired voice are cheap to try and easy to change.

question: Answers lack facts that live only in private files. Next rung?
answers: Write a longer prompt
Fine-tune the model on those files
Add retrieval over those files
Raise the temperature
fact: Missing knowledge is what RAG is for. Fine-tuning changes habits, not facts, and goes stale as the files change.

question: Prompts and RAG work, but 10,000 daily outputs must match a strict style. Next?
answers: Add many more documents to the index
Ask staff to edit each output
Increase top-k
Consider fine-tuning on examples
fact: A consistent style at scale is where fine-tuning earns its place, once cheaper rungs have been tried and measured against a baseline.

question: Best starting material for a support eval?
answers: Real past tickets with good replies
Questions the vendor wrote
Public benchmark questions
Easy questions made up for the demo run
fact: Real tickets show how customers actually write. A test set from your own work tells you more than any generic benchmark.

question: Building an eval from 100 tickets. What should you add on purpose?
answers: The most common ticket types
Hard and out-of-scope cases
Tickets that closed smoothly
The shortest, tidiest tickets
fact: Easy cases flatter every model. Tricky and refusal cases show where it breaks, and the cost of those failures is what the customer cares about.

question: Who should write the "good answer" for each ticket in an eval?
answers: The vendor sales team
The model being tested
The experts who handle tickets
Whoever happens to be free that day
fact: The reference answer should reflect real standards. If the model writes its own, the test just marks its own homework.

question: What does comparing two models fairly require?
answers: Each vendor picks the questions
One run and a gut feel
Comparing price lists only
Same prompts, data and grading
fact: Change one thing at a time. Identical test cases and scoring let the difference come from the model, not from the setup.

question: Model B scores higher but needs a very different prompt. What is fair?
answers: Tune a prompt for each model
Reuse model A prompt for both
Pick the cheaper model unseen
Trust the higher public score
fact: A prompt written for one model can undersell another. Give each a fair effort at tuning, then compare on the same test set.

question: A provider updates a model and answers shift. What catches it?
answers: Reading the release notes alone
Rerun your eval on the new version
Waiting for users to report oddities
Checking the invoice totals
fact: Model updates can change behaviour on your tasks. A saved eval set turns "it feels different" into a score you can compare before and after.

question: In an API build, how do you guard against surprise model changes?
answers: Use the newest one automatically
Pin a version, then test upgrades
Freeze prompts and skip upgrades
Skip tests when scores were high
fact: Pinning keeps behaviour steady while you test a newer version on your eval. Upgrade when the scores say it is safe.

question: Which belongs in a pilot success criterion?
answers: A list of favourite features
A promise of full rollout this year
The vendor roadmap
A measure, baseline and target
fact: "Cut handling time from 10 minutes to 6" can be checked. Vague hopes cannot, and they make the pilot hard to turn into a decision.

question: A pilot saved time but quality dipped. Is it a success?
answers: Check against the agreed criteria
Yes, speed is what matters
No, any dip means failure
Extend it until the numbers look better
fact: Success was defined before the pilot. If the criteria set a quality floor, judge against it; if not, agree the trade-off with the owner.

question: Evals show 98% on routine refunds and 70% on complaints. Best next step?
answers: Ease review on all tickets
Ease review on refunds only
Keep full review everywhere forever
Ease review on complaints first
fact: Reduce human review where evidence supports it and keep it where errors are costly or results are weaker, then keep watching.

question: What should still go to a person even when evals look strong?
answers: Spelling and grammar clean-up work
Table formatting
High-stakes or one-way decisions
Routine greetings
fact: Strong scores lower risk but do not remove it. Where a mistake is costly or cannot be undone, a human check stays in place.

question: Scoring retrieval and answers separately shows where the fault lies.
fact: A wrong answer can come from missing passages or from how the model used them. Separate scores point you to the right fix.

question: Limiting which tools an agent may call is a kind of guardrail.
fact: Guardrails sit at input, retrieval, output and action stages. Least-privilege tools and human approval for irreversible actions are the action-stage ones.

question: A prompt tweak fixed one complaint but the eval score fell. Lesson?
answers: Revert whenever one case fails
Ignore the score; the fix is visible
Evals only suit new models
Fixes can break other cases
fact: An eval covers many cases at once, so it shows side effects that one fix hides. Keep the tweak only if the whole set improves.

question: A customer wants "95% accurate". What must you ask?
answers: Accurate on what, graded by whom?
Which model is biggest?
How many users sign in?
What is the monthly budget for it?
fact: A percentage means nothing until you know the test set and the grader. Turning it into a defined eval is what makes the target real.

question: An eval has 20 cases and all passed. Safe to drop human review?
answers: Yes, a perfect score settles the matter
No: too few cases to show reliability
Yes, if the model is the newest
No, review can never be removed
fact: Twenty cases cannot cover real variety. Build a larger, more varied set and watch live results before easing review.
